topic.subject: maths
topic.title: Rational numbers
topic.scope: rational numbers, standard form, comparing, operations, properties, rational numbers between two numbers

nodes.name: Meaning and forms of rational numbers
Definition of a rational number
A rational number is p/q with integers p, q and q not 0
Every integer and whole number is rational (n = n/1)
Denominator cannot be zero; 0/q = 0
Equivalent forms and standard form
Multiplying or dividing numerator and denominator by the same non-zero integer gives an equivalent rational
Standard form has a positive denominator and HCF 1
Negative rationals and the number line
-a/b, a/(-b) and -(a/b) are the same number, lying left of zero
Marking p/q on the number line by dividing unit lengths (improper values lie beyond 1)
Comparing and rationals between two numbers
Comparing rational numbers
Compare using a common positive denominator, then compare numerators
For negative rationals, larger magnitude means smaller value
Rational numbers between two rationals
There are infinitely many rationals between any two rationals
Find them by writing equivalent forms with larger denominators or by taking the mean
Operations and properties
Addition and subtraction
Add after making denominators equal; add only numerators
Subtraction is adding the additive inverse
Multiplication and division
Multiply numerators together and denominators together
Divide by multiplying by the reciprocal of the divisor; 0 has no reciprocal
Properties of operations
external_prereqs: properties of whole numbers and integers

nodes.name: Closure: rationals are closed under +, -, x but not under division
Commutative and associative hold for + and x, not for - and division
Identities (0 and 1), additive inverse and reciprocal are different ideas

misconceptions.statement: A rational number must have a positive numerator and a positive denominator, so -3/4 is not a rational number.
misconceptions.why: Students meet fractions first as positive parts of a whole and carry that picture over.
misconceptions.fix: A rational number is p/q with p and q any integers and q not zero, so -3/4 and 3/(-4) are rational.

probe.question: Is -3/4 a rational number? Yes or no, and why?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because a fraction cannot have a negative number in it.

misconceptions.root_belief: a new number set is just the old one

misconceptions.statement: The integer 5 is not a rational number because it has no denominator.
misconceptions.why: Students think rational numbers must visibly look like a fraction.
misconceptions.fix: Every integer n can be written as n/1, so every integer is a rational number.

probe.question: Is 5 a rational number?
probe.wrong_answer: No, 5 is a whole number and rational numbers are fractions.

misconceptions.root_belief: a number must look a certain way to belong
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student understanding of rational number sets and their representations

misconceptions.statement: Zero is not a rational number because it means nothing.
misconceptions.why: Zero is felt to be an absence rather than a real number to be divided.
misconceptions.fix: 0 can be written as 0/1, 0/5 and so on, so it is a rational number.
misconceptions.root_belief: zero means nothing, so it is not a number

misconceptions.statement: 5/0 equals 0 because nothing is left to share.
misconceptions.why: Students treat division by zero as sharing among no one and give the answer zero.
misconceptions.fix: Division by zero is not defined, so a rational number can never have 0 as its denominator.
misconceptions.root_belief: zero always gives a zero result
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student errors with division by zero

misconceptions.statement: 0/5 is undefined because it has a zero in it.
misconceptions.why: Students hear that zero is forbidden in fractions and apply it to the numerator too.
misconceptions.fix: 0/5 = 0 since 0 shared among 5 is 0; only a zero denominator is not allowed.
misconceptions.root_belief: a special symbol ruins whatever it appears in
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student errors with zero in division

misconceptions.statement: Adding the same number to the numerator and denominator gives an equivalent rational number.
misconceptions.why: Students keep 'do the same to both parts' but use addition rather than multiplication.
misconceptions.fix: Only multiplying or dividing both parts by the same non-zero integer keeps the value; adding changes it.

probe.question: Add 2 to the numerator and denominator of 1/3. Is the result equal to 1/3?

misconceptions.root_belief: doing the same to both parts keeps the value
misconceptions.source_hint: research on additive versus multiplicative reasoning in rational number

misconceptions.statement: 1/2 and 2/4 are different numbers because their digits are different.
misconceptions.why: Students treat fractions as pairs of whole numbers, not as one quantity.
misconceptions.fix: 1/2 and 2/4 name the same point on the number line, so they are the same rational number.

probe.question: Are 1/2 and 2/4 the same rational number?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because 1 and 2 are not the same as 2 and 4.

misconceptions.root_belief: different symbols mean different numbers
misconceptions.source_hint: research on equivalent fractions and fractions as numbers

misconceptions.statement: 3/(-4) is already in standard form because 3 and 4 have no common factor.
misconceptions.why: Students check only the HCF and forget the denominator must be positive.
misconceptions.fix: Standard form needs a positive denominator, so 3/(-4) is written as -3/4.

probe.question: Write 3/(-4) in standard form.
probe.wrong_answer: It is already in standard form.

misconceptions.root_belief: the sign's position does not matter

misconceptions.statement: Dividing numerator and denominator by any common factor gives the standard form, so 12/18 becomes 6/9.
misconceptions.why: Students stop after the first cancelling step.
misconceptions.fix: Divide by the HCF so that nothing common remains: 12/18 = 2/3.
misconceptions.root_belief: the first step of a procedure is enough
misconceptions.source_hint: classroom studies of simplification of fractions

misconceptions.statement: -3/4 and 3/(-4) are different numbers, and 3/(-4) is positive.
misconceptions.why: Students assume the sign belongs only to the numerator, or that two signs cancel.
misconceptions.fix: -3/4, 3/(-4) and -(3/4) are all the same negative number.

probe.question: Is 3/(-4) positive or negative?
probe.wrong_answer: Positive, because the 4 is in the denominator.

misconceptions.root_belief: where a sign is written changes the number

misconceptions.statement: Every positive rational number lies between 0 and 1.
misconceptions.why: Fractions are always drawn as parts of one whole.
misconceptions.fix: Rationals like 5/3 or 7/2 are greater than 1 and lie further right on the number line.

probe.question: Where does 5/3 lie on the number line?
probe.wrong_answer: Between 0 and 1, at the fifth mark.

misconceptions.root_belief: a fraction is only a part of one whole
misconceptions.source_hint: research on fraction number-line representations

misconceptions.statement: The rational number with the larger denominator is larger, so 1/8 is greater than 1/5.
misconceptions.why: Whole-number size is applied to the digits in the denominator.
misconceptions.fix: A larger denominator splits the whole into smaller parts, so 1/8 is less than 1/5.
misconceptions.root_belief: bigger digits in a symbol mean bigger value
misconceptions.source_hint: research on whole number bias in comparing fractions

misconceptions.statement: To compare fractions with different denominators, just compare the numerators, so 5/9 is greater than 4/5.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the numerator and denominator as separate numbers and ignore the denominator.
misconceptions.fix: Make the denominators equal first (4/5 = 36/45 and 5/9 = 25/45), then compare numerators, so 4/5 is greater.
misconceptions.root_belief: the parts of a symbol can be judged separately
misconceptions.source_hint: research on fraction comparison strategies

misconceptions.statement: -1/2 is greater than -1/4 because 1/2 is greater than 1/4.
misconceptions.why: Students ignore the minus sign and compare sizes only.
misconceptions.fix: On the number line -1/2 is to the left of -1/4, so -1/2 is smaller than -1/4.
misconceptions.root_belief: ignore the sign; size of digits decides
misconceptions.source_hint: research on ordering negative numbers

misconceptions.statement: There is no rational number between 1/5 and 2/5, because 1 and 2 are consecutive.
misconceptions.why: Students expect every number to have a next neighbour, as whole numbers do.
misconceptions.fix: Between any two rationals there are more, e.g. 1/5 = 10/50 and 2/5 = 20/50 with 11/50 to 19/50 between them.

probe.question: Name a rational number between 1/5 and 2/5.

misconceptions.root_belief: every number has a next neighbour
misconceptions.source_hint: research on discreteness versus density of rational numbers

misconceptions.statement: Between two rationals there are only a limited number of rationals.
misconceptions.why: Students think a short stretch of the number line can hold only finitely many things.
misconceptions.fix: However close two rationals are, there are infinitely many rationals between them.

probe.question: How many rationals lie between 0 and 1/100?
probe.wrong_answer: Only a few, as the gap is tiny.

misconceptions.root_belief: a small interval holds only finitely many items
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student concepts of infinity and density

misconceptions.why: Students add the top and bottom separately like two whole-number pairs.
misconceptions.fix: Make the denominators equal first and then add only the numerators: 1/2 + 1/3 = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.
misconceptions.root_belief: operate on the parts separately, like whole numbers
misconceptions.source_hint: well-documented fraction addition error in classroom research

misconceptions.statement: After making the denominators equal, you also add the denominators: 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/12.
misconceptions.why: Students follow a procedure where every number in sight is added.
misconceptions.fix: The common denominator stays the same because it names the size of the part: 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6.
misconceptions.root_belief: every number in an expression gets operated on
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of fraction addition errors

misconceptions.statement: Subtracting a negative rational makes the answer smaller: 1/2 - (-1/3) = 1/6.
misconceptions.why: Students believe subtraction always reduces a number.
misconceptions.fix: Subtracting a rational means adding its additive inverse, so 1/2 - (-1/3) = 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6.
misconceptions.root_belief: subtraction always makes things smaller
misconceptions.source_hint: research on integer and rational subtraction with negatives

misconceptions.statement: Multiplying always gives a bigger number, so (1/2) x (1/3) is bigger than 1/2.
misconceptions.why: Whole-number multiplication always increases, and students generalise.
misconceptions.fix: Multiplying by a rational between 0 and 1 gives a smaller number: (1/2) x (1/3) = 1/6.

probe.question: Is (1/2) x (1/3) greater or smaller than 1/2?
probe.wrong_answer: Greater, because multiplication makes numbers bigger.

misconceptions.root_belief: multiplication always makes things bigger
misconceptions.source_hint: research on multiplication makes bigger misconception

misconceptions.statement: To multiply rationals you need a common denominator and keep it: 2/5 x 3/5 = 6/5.
misconceptions.why: The common-denominator rule from addition is applied to every operation.
misconceptions.fix: Multiply numerators and denominators directly: 2/5 x 3/5 = 6/25.
misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one operation works for all
misconceptions.source_hint: research on fraction multiplication errors

misconceptions.statement: Dividing always gives a smaller number, so (3/4) / (1/2) is less than 3/4.
misconceptions.why: Whole-number division by numbers above 1 always reduces the result.
misconceptions.fix: Dividing by a rational less than 1 gives a bigger number: (3/4) / (1/2) = 3/2.

probe.question: Is (3/4) / (1/2) greater or smaller than 3/4?
probe.wrong_answer: Smaller, because division makes numbers smaller.

misconceptions.root_belief: division always makes things smaller
misconceptions.source_hint: research on division makes smaller misconception

misconceptions.statement: To divide by a rational, flip the first one: (2/3) / (4/5) = (3/2) x (4/5).
misconceptions.why: Students remember 'flip and multiply' without knowing which fraction to flip.
misconceptions.fix: Flip only the divisor: (2/3) / (4/5) = (2/3) x (5/4) = 5/6.
misconceptions.root_belief: a remembered step can be applied to any item
misconceptions.source_hint: research on invert-and-multiply errors

misconceptions.statement: Dividing any two rational numbers always gives a rational number.
misconceptions.why: Closure holds for +, - and x, so students assume it holds for division too.
misconceptions.fix: Division is not closed: any rational divided by 0 is not defined, so the result is not always a rational number.

probe.question: Is the division of two rational numbers always a rational number?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a rational divided by a rational is rational.

misconceptions.root_belief: a property holding for some cases holds for all

misconceptions.statement: Subtraction is commutative: 1/2 - 1/3 equals 1/3 - 1/2.
misconceptions.why: Commutativity of addition is applied to every operation.
misconceptions.fix: Only addition and multiplication are commutative; 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6 but 1/3 - 1/2 = -1/6.

probe.question: Is 1/2 - 1/3 equal to 1/3 - 1/2?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the order does not matter.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one operation works for all operations
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student understanding of algebraic properties

misconceptions.statement: The additive inverse of 3/4 is 4/3.
misconceptions.why: Students think 'inverse' always means turning the fraction upside down.
misconceptions.fix: The additive inverse of 3/4 is -3/4, since 3/4 + (-3/4) = 0; 4/3 is the reciprocal.

probe.question: What is the additive inverse of 3/4?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of confusion between additive and multiplicative inverse

misconceptions.statement: The additive identity is 1 and the multiplicative identity is 0.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up which number leaves the value unchanged for which operation.
misconceptions.fix: Adding 0 leaves a number unchanged, so 0 is the additive identity; multiplying by 1 leaves it unchanged, so 1 is the multiplicative identity.

probe.question: What is the additive identity for rational numbers?

misconceptions.root_belief: one special number serves every operation
